## Motivation

The single most arresting fact about C-section use in Bangladesh between 2004 and 2022 is the *speed* of change. The national rate quintupled and crossed every WHO and public-health benchmark in less than fifteen years. Before any causal analysis is attempted, the reader needs to see the trajectory itself.

The WHO's 2015 statement on caesarean section rates [@who2015csection] cautions that population-level rates above 10–15% are not associated with maternal or neonatal benefit, and may be associated with harm. Bangladesh crossed 15% in 2010, 30% in 2016, and 40% in 2020.

## Data and setup

Wave-level trajectory data come from the descriptive aggregation in `data/processed/descriptive/P1_Csec_Trends_All.csv` (Bangladesh, India, Pakistan together) and the threshold-crossing year estimates in `data/processed/descriptive/P1_Threshold_Years.csv`.

```{r}
#| label: load-trends
trends <- load_csec_trends()
trends |> book_table(digits = 1)
```

## Interpretation

Two observations matter for the rest of the book. First, Bangladesh's trajectory is *steeper* than India's or Pakistan's at every wave — by 2022, Bangladesh's C-section rate exceeds India's by roughly 20 percentage points despite India's much larger health-system base. Second, the 2011 wave is the inflection: pre-2011, the slope is gentler; post-2011, it accelerates and reaches its modern level by 2017–18.

The brief calls the post-2011 era *demand-driven*: rates above WHO's safety ceiling, private-sector concentration, social-norm propagation. The supply-constrained era — emergency-only, scarcity-driven — is what's left of the pre-2011 BDHS waves. Whether a single instrument identifies a single treatment effect across this regime change is precisely the question Part II forces.
